hypotheses.justification: The statement also holds for N = 0, so the hypothesis can be dropped. For N = 0 we have primeFactors 0 = ∅, so both products are 1. The claim becomes (Gamma0 0).index = 0, because the right side is 0 * 1 = 0. Gamma0 0 is the subgroup of matrices in SL₂(ℤ) with lower-left entry c ≡ 0 mod 0, that is c = 0. It has infinite index. The matrices gₙ = [[1,0],[n,1]] have first columns (1,n). Left cosets g·Γ₀(0) are determined by the first column of g up to sign, because g·Γ₀(0) = g'·Γ₀(0) iff g⁻¹g' has c = 0 iff g'e₁ = ±g e₁. The first columns (1,n) are pairwise distinct up to sign, so the gₙ lie in infinitely many distinct cosets. Mathlib's `Subgroup.index` is 0 for infinite index, so the claim holds. For the proof, split on N = 0. When N ≠ 0, use the existing proof. When N = 0, simp reduces the goal to `(Gamma0 0).index = 0`, which follows from the infinite-index argument above, for example via `Subgroup.index_eq_zero_iff_infinite` or `Subgroup.finiteIndex_iff` plus an injection ℕ → SL₂(ℤ)/Γ₀(0). I did not run Lean to check this.
